units: a herder explains that his flock stopped feeding
he blames the change on the wetness of the vegetation
a woman who keeps animals nearby describes a different reaction in her own stock
the goats crowded against the fence
the herder admits he moved the watering point
the shade of the hedge made the water too cold to drink
the young animals drank less and lost weight
the herder judges that the fault is his own and not the weather's
the woman nearby confesses she made the same mistake earlier
text: The shepherd said his flock had stopped grazing the moment the wind picked up. He put it down to wet grass, which sits heavy in the mouth, and to the way an uneasy animal chews badly. The woman on the far slope, who keeps goats, told him hers had done the opposite: they crowded up against the fence and stayed there. At that the shepherd owned up. He had shifted the water trough closer to the hedge, and the shade there kept the water cold. Since the move, he said, the lambs drank less, lost weight, and their mothers wore themselves out calling them back. The blame lay with his own hand, he decided, and not with the weather. She laughed quietly at the confession, then admitted she had done the very same thing in the cold season before, and had watched it end the same way.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: harnessing a draft animal pressed on its throat
that pressure got in the way of the animal's breathing
the animal could not deliver its full power
craftsmen shifted the bearing onto the shoulders by means of a padded collar
this change raised the load the animal could pull
a head piece served to steer the animal without injuring it
a guard over the mouth kept the handlers safe from bites
these inventions spread from one valley to the next by copying
text: In earlier times, harnessing a draft animal ran up against a blunt mechanical problem, and it went unsolved for a long while. The strap crossed the throat, and the harder the beast pulled, the tighter it squeezed the windpipe. Breathing gave out before the load had properly moved, so most of the animal's strength was simply thrown away. The remedy lay in moving the point that took the strain. Craftsmen built a padded collar to rest on the shoulders, which let the animal breathe freely while it pulled, and the weight it could shift rose sharply. A soft head piece came next, giving the driver a way to steer without cutting into the muzzle, and a light guard over the mouth kept handlers clear of bites during awkward turns. Workshops copied one another from valley to valley, and the design traveled on with no name attached to it.

units: birds and mammals feed their young in different ways
nestlings come out of the egg almost bare
a fine insulating down protects them from the cold
the parent birds carry food in from outside the nest
these trips back and forth are very frequent
young mammals take a food made by their mother
young mammals press against one another to keep their heat
both methods answer the same feeding need
text: Set a clutch of hatchlings beside a litter of young mammals and what you see is two different answers worked out for one and the same demand. In the nest, the chicks break out of the shell almost bare, and only a thin, insulating down stands between their skin and the cold. Every mouthful has to be carried in from outside, so the parents shuttle back and forth from first light until dark, with barely a pause between one trip and the next. Among mammals the food comes from the mother's own body, so it is there whenever it is wanted, and no journey is needed to fetch it. The young pile in against one another and hold on to their heat while the adults are away. What differs, then, is where the food comes from and how far the parents have to roam. The need being met is exactly the same on either side.

units: a naturalist made an inventory of the shelters on a wooded slope
a tunnel dug under a stump housed a rodent
she never once caught sight of that occupant
a hollow under roots served as a den for a carnivore
birds had built their nests in the cracks of a fallen wall
insects lived under the loosened bark of dead trunks
the shelters changed occupants over the course of the season
she handed her notes to a research team, which published them
text: A naturalist spent her days on a wooded slope, setting down in a list every shelter she could find and whatever was housed in it. She began with the burrows that had been cut into the hillside. One of them opened under a rotting stump and belonged to a rodent she never once laid eyes on. Further along she found a den wedged beneath a knot of roots, lined with hair and dry twigs, and in use by a carnivore of middling size. Then came the cracks in a fallen wall, packed with birds' nests, and the loose bark of dead trunks, alive underneath with insects too small to count. What struck her hardest of all was the turnover of the tenants. A shelter left empty was taken over again before the season was out. She handed her notes over to a research team, and they put the whole lot into print without delay.

units: you must first pick a spot sheltered from the wind
the feeder is fixed high up, out of reach of predators
dry seed is poured into it
salty leftovers must be kept out
a shallow dish of water is set beside it
the water must be changed as soon as it turns cloudy
the feeder must be washed regularly to stop disease from spreading
the animals should be watched from a distance without going closer
the feeding must not be broken off suddenly in the cold season
text: So you want to feed the birds in the orchard, and you would rather do it properly than badly. Start by finding a corner out of the wind, open enough to see across, and awkward for a cat to climb. Hang the feeder high, well clear of any low branch, then fill it with dry seed. Never any salty scraps left over from a meal. Set a shallow dish of water beside it, a wide saucer will do, and change the water the moment it turns cloudy. Every other week, scrub the whole thing out with hot water, because droppings build up and pass disease along, and a dirty feeder does more harm than no feeder at all. Watch your visitors from a distance and stay back, or they will quit the orchard altogether. One last thing, and it matters more than the rest: once the cold season has set in, do not cut the food off all at once.

units: the level of a body of water fell after a dry season
a strip of mud linking the shore to the islet was laid bare
predators from the land took that crossing
the nests set on the ground were raided
the adult birds abandoned the breeding site
part of the colony settled on a steep bank
the wardens had a channel cut to isolate the islet
some pairs came back to lay the following season
the original numbers were never recovered
text: A dry season pulled the water level down, and that drop on its own was enough to undo the whole bird colony that had been nesting on the islet out in the middle. As it fell back, the water laid bare a tongue of mud running from the shore out to the islet, and carnivores prowling the edge were across it on the first night. Nests sitting on open ground were raided, the eggs lost, and the adults walked away from a site their kind had used for generations. Part of the colony moved to a steep rocky bank, harder to reach but open to the spray, where almost nothing hatched. Volunteers raised the alarm, and the wardens who look after the place had a narrow channel cut, so that the islet could no longer be reached on foot. The next season some pairs came back to lay. The old numbers, though, were never seen again.

units: a shelter is dug into a bank between roots
brambles hide its entrance
the rains used to flood the tunnel
the soaked bedding turned icy for the animal
a second opening was cut higher up the bank
a dry chamber was hollowed out above the level the water reached
dry grass lines the floor of that chamber
the old tunnel now carries the rain away
text: Low in the bank a dark mouth runs in between the roots, screened so well by brambles that a walker would go straight past and notice nothing. The passage slopes down, its walls rubbed smooth by fur going through, over and over. When the rains came, water ran along the slope and gathered at the bottom of the tunnel. The soaked bedding turned icy, and the animal lay shivering on it. So a second mouth was cut higher up the bank, and from there a shaft climbed to a dry chamber, hollowed out above the line the water had reached. Brittle grass, dragged in from the meadow next door, covers the floor of it now, and the warmth of a sleeping body holds there without trouble. The old passage carries the rain instead, swallowing it and letting it out lower down, well away from the bed.

units: the writer compares rearing in a closed space and rearing on open range
a closed space makes each animal easy to tell apart and to examine
an injury is picked up early there
confinement helps parasites move around
open range builds up the muscle of the animals
open range cuts down joint trouble
the scattering of the animals makes health checks hard
the writer advises running both systems by age and by season
he asks that the choice rest on measurements and not on beliefs
text: Pitting closed housing against open range settles very little in the end, and the demand from both camps for a single verdict only coarsens the argument. Shut in, an animal can be told apart from the rest, weighed, handled, looked over, and a wound shows up while it is still small. That same closeness gathers parasites and hands them around the herd. Out on open ground the account turns over: muscle builds, joints give less trouble, but the animals scatter, and keeping a check on their health becomes a matter of luck. A sensible holding will run both systems, then, sorting the stock by age and by season instead of raising either method into doctrine. What is still wanting is the habit of settling such choices by what has been measured, and not by what the keeper happens to believe in his own heart.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running a care center looks after injured animals
she worked as a veterinary assistant before setting up her shelter
the shelter sits in an abandoned farm
she feeds the nestlings with tweezers at short intervals
she holds fractured wings still and watches them mend
she teaches volunteers to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it
she writes down every arrival in a register
she releases the healed animals well away from busy roads
she refuses to give a name to the animals she takes in
text: The woman who runs the care center gives her days to animals that will never be hers. She started out as a veterinary assistant, learning how to hold a struggling creature, how to set a splint, how to read a picture of a broken bone, and later she opened her own shelter in a farm that had stood empty for years. The work falls into fixed tasks. She feeds the nestlings with tweezers, a little at a time, from first light until dusk. She binds broken wings, watches the weight come back onto them, changes the dressings. She trains volunteers, showing them how to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it or getting bitten. She writes down every arrival in a thick register: the species, the injury, how it ended. The ones that mend she lets go well away from busy roads, and she gives none of them a name.

units: a factual book about animals that live by night is assessed
the opening sets down observations made in the field
that opening convinces the reviewer
the middle chapters lay out measurements from work on captive animals
that part is judged too dry to read
it still brings solid knowledge about hearing and finding one's way
the closing pages give protective recommendations that stay too vague
the drawn plates are held to be the great success of the book
the reviewer advises reading it all the same
text: The book opens with notebooks kept after dark, and that opening wins you over at once. The author waits out long stretches for nothing, sets down hopes that come to nothing, and records brief meetings with animals that sense her long before she can make them out. Then the tone shifts. The middle chapters lay out run after run of measurements taken from captive animals, in prose so dry that the reading bogs down completely. Solid material sits in there all the same, on hearing and on how such animals find their way. The closing pages offer a list of protective measures, too broad, unhappily, to commit anyone to anything. The drawn plates are another matter: they catch posture and movement so well that they carry the book on their own. Worth reading, then, soft middle and all.
